home.purpose: This site presents my Round 2 recruitment submission for The Neural Network, the AI club at IIM Sirmaur. It shows one year programme, From Zero to Shipped, in two parts. Curation and Research covers what members learn and make across 24 sessions. Outreach and External Relations covers who the club works with and how it asks.

curationOverview.lead: A 24-session year, two sessions a month, in four terms of six. Each term is harder than the last, and the first session of every term is still one a beginner can walk into.
rules: Twenty-four sessions in four terms. Three learning sessions are followed by one play session, giving six play sessions (4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24).
Sessions run 60 to 90 minutes. Session 17 runs about two hours and Session 23 is a full day.

No coding in the core. The most technical material (APIs, terminals, GitHub and Vercel deployment, RAG and fine-tuning in depth) is held in the optional Maker Track so the core stays open to every BMS student.
Three levels: Explorer (a browser and curiosity), Builder (no-code tools and spreadsheets) and Maker (plugs AI into other software).
Entry sessions assume no account, laptop or prior knowledge. Session 1 runs on members' own phones.
Rooms for 30 to 80 people seated in fours. The plan works with twelve people at one table.
Free tools only, checked a week before and 24 hours before. Every activity has a paper or no-tool version.
The core 24 sessions never depend on an outside partner. If a partner declines, the session runs as written.
curationOverview.leagueNote: These weights are a starting guess. The document says to review them after the first four sessions. Points are capped at 40 per member per session so that no one runs away with the board. Awards are peer-voted: Curious Cat, Best Explainer, Faceplant Hero, Team Player, Rising Star, People's Choice.

why: The audience is a management cohort, not a coding cohort. A business-school club that starts with code or model internals loses the people who most need it. The programme therefore ties each session to a student problem (a case pack, a messy sheet, a mess menu, a placement) and teaches building only in service of a business problem.
Most students already use AI, but few can explain or check it. The year starts from daily use and builds the habits of questioning and verification before any automation or agent work.

The club must survive real conditions. Speakers cancel, wifi fails, exams arrive, turnout shrinks in week nine. The plan therefore names its fallbacks, uses free tools and paper versions, and does not depend on any external partner for its core calendar.

Outreach earns its place when it gives students something specific. The strongest outreach pitches a defined workshop, case challenge or clinic with a clear owner and output, instead of asking for logos or generic sponsorship.

A single, coordinated programme beats parallel ones. Curation needs speakers, judges, problem statements and prizes that only Outreach can supply; Outreach needs session content, recaps and demos that only Curation can create. Part 4 sets out that interlock.
mission: Teach AI to absolute beginners through problems they already have, with every session producing something they keep.
Build critical, responsible AI users who verify claims, protect personal data and keep their own judgement.
Give every member a route from first prompt to a shipped project, with mentors, peers and public demo days along the way.
Connect the club to industry practitioners, alumni, professional bodies, peer clubs and platforms through honest, small, well-run collaborations.
Run the whole programme on free tools and on student time, so that it survives exams, absent speakers and a changing tool landscape.

whyReachable: Order by speed of reply, not by prestige. The document tests every name against four questions: Is there a visible reason to engage? Is there a published channel? Does the club have something specific to offer? Is the ask small?
Skip global giants whose outreach dies in a PR inbox.
Peers say yes faster than companies. A fellow IIM is a lighter collaboration than a company.
Start with campus bodies, the alumni cell and professional bodies reached through a disclosed introduction (Tier 1). Famous names are Tier 5 and come only after a pilot has produced evidence.
offer: A well-scoped way to meet curious management students: a defined workshop, case challenge or clinic with a clear owner and output.
The club's edge is a management lens. Students work out how an AI tool makes money, fits into an enterprise workflow or scales across tier-2 markets.
A named thank-you, a short report with photographs and anonymous feedback, and an honest user perspective.
A pilot first (one session, one challenge, one clinic). The club earns the right to ask for recurring support only after the pilot works.

sustain: Zero-cost core. Free tools, student-run sessions and paper fallbacks mean the programme does not stop when a sponsor or tool does.
Knowledge that outlives members. Field Guide v2.0, session records, ledger and slips become the handover pack; the next team starts from what happened, not from opinion.
Peer teaching builds the next team. Member-led segments in later sessions and whole member-led sessions in year two; Duo Swap and Spotlight create presenters; Maker Track creates mentors.
Diversified partners. A pipeline of about forty targets across five tiers; no partner is on the critical path. Relationships are recorded in the ledger, not in individuals' inboxes.
Annual signature events. Neural Fest and Demo Day become the yearly anchor once approved.
Annual refresh. Mid-year review and annual partner review prune weak sessions and weak leads (V2-15).
Year-two ideas already identified. Member-led sessions, a second Maker cohort, a Year-2 learning menu voted by members, and the next batch of mentors recruited at the finale.

Make the club visible: consistent recaps, a content engine and a few well-chosen media relationships.
Run every contact with integrity: faculty-advisor approval, verified contacts, honest claims, one follow-up, a thank-you and a report.
